text_blocks.snippet: Both ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) inhibitors and ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers) are considered equivalent first-line treatments for high blood pressure (hypertension).
snippet_highlighted_words: Both ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) inhibitors and ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers) are considered equivalent first-line treatments for high blood pressure (hypertension)

list.snippet: Effectiveness: Both classes target the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) to relax blood vessels, lower blood pressure, and protect the heart and kidneys . Large studies show they have essentially identical long-term effectiveness in preventing major cardiovascular events like heart attacks and strokes.

Shared Contraindications: Neither class is safe to use during pregnancy (due to the risk of birth defects), and they should never be combined together due to increased risks of high potassium and kidney damage.

Side Effects (Cough): ACE inhibitors (such as lisinopril or enalapril) block the breakdown of bradykinin, which causes a persistent, dry, nagging cough in about 5% to 20% of users. ARBs (such as losartan or valsartan) do not affect bradykinin and rarely cause this cough.
Angioedema: ACE inhibitors carry a small risk of angioedema (swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat), which happens more often in individuals of African descent. ARBs have a much lower risk.

Track Record vs. Cost: ACE inhibitors have a longer clinical history and extensive trial data, while ARBs generally offer superior patient tolerability (fewer discontinuations) and are now widely available as affordable generics.

text_blocks.snippet: Many clinicians lean toward ARBs first because patients tolerate them better with fewer side effects. However, if you already take an ACE inhibitor like lisinopril and are doing well without a cough, there is usually no need to switch. If a dry cough develops on an ACE inhibitor, doctors typically transition the patient directly to an ARB.
